extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, fact-checkers, and public-health communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes false and misleading claims about COVID-19 and provides corrective public-health guidance and context (e.g., on prevention, treatments, vaccines, and social effects). Intended to identify misinformation and state authoritative recommendations or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonality claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that warm weather (spring/summer/tropical temperatures) will end or prevent COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flu is seasonal in some countries but not others; while COVID-19 may show seasonality this has not been determined. COVID-19 has not bypassed tropical locations; it seems to be transmissible in all climates, and has seriously affected many warm-climate countries (example: Dubai). Do not assume warm weather protects against transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outbreak risk in cruise ships/close quarters
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements minimizing risk of COVID-19 transmission on cruise ships or similar settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outbreaks on cruise ships — where an older population lives in close quarters and frequently touch shared surfaces — were common, illustrating high transmission risk in such environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breastfeeding during COVID-19
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice on whether women should breastfeed if they have confirmed or suspected COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WHO and UNICEF advise that women should continue to breastfeed during the COVID-19 pandemic even if they have confirmed or suspected COVID-19. Evidence (as of May 2020) indicates it is unlikely COVID-19 can be transmitted through breast milk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual transmission and effects on fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about SARS-CoV-2 transmission via semen and effects on male fertility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SARS-CoV-2 can persist in men's semen even after recovery though the virus cannot replicate in the reproductive system. Some studies found viral RNA in semen but sexual transmission remains uncertain; fever during infection can reduce sperm counts (azoospermia/oligospermia) via heat or viral testicular infection. Treat claims of sexual transmission and fertility impact cautiously pending robust evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handwashing as primary preventive measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations about washing hands to prevent COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washing in soap and water for at least 20 seconds is the best way to clean hands. If soap and water are not available, use a hand sanitizer that is at least 60% alcohol unless hands are visibly dirty or greasy. This guidance comes from CDC and public-health authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness and proper use of hand sanitizer
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that hand sanitizer is ineffective because it is 'antibacterial not antiviral', or that sanitizers don't inactivate SARS-CoV-2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness depends on ingredients; most commercially sold hand sanitizers inactivate SARS-CoV-2. Hand sanitizer is recommended when soap and water are unavailable, though it is not effective against all types of germs. Plain soap is recommended over antibacterial soaps; antibacterial soaps show no evidence of superiority and may have long-term downsides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use of face masks
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about whether masks work for the general public and whether authorities' mask messaging was accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (especially in Asia) recommended mask wearing early; in other places messaging conflicted initially. Evidence supports masks can limit spread; some early anti-mask messages were driven by shortages rather than science. Media misinterpretations of studies (e.g., neck gaiters) should be scrutinized: single-study results do not generalize across materials and designs. False claims that masks cause low blood oxygen, high CO2, weakened immunity, or antibiotic-resistant pneumonia are unsubstantiated. Legal-exemption claims (e.g., blanket ADA exemptions) are incorrect; DOJ states ADA does not provide blanket exemption and fraudulent 'exemption' cards have circulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcohol consumption myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that drinking alcohol protects against COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drinking alcohol does not protect against COVID-19 and increases short- and long-term health risks. Consumption of non-consumable alcohols (methanol, isopropanol) is poisonous; methanol poisonings and deaths occurred in countries where false beliefs circulated. Do not ingest disinfectants or non-beverage alcohol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tobacco and nicotine claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that tobacco smoking prevents COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early small observational findings suggested an inverse relationship but larger and more recent evidence shows smokers have increased risk of infection and more severe respiratory symptoms. Do not rely on or promote tobacco as protective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illicit drug myths (e.g., cocaine snorting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Viral claims that snorting cocaine or similar acts sterilize the nostrils against SARS-CoV-2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These claims are false and harmful. Public-health agencies have explicitly debunked them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm or hot drinks preventing infection
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that drinking warm drinks (e.g., ~30°C/86°F or hotter) kills the virus and prevents COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WHO made no recommendation to 'drink many hot drinks' to kill the virus. Drinking hot water can damage oral mucosa. Do not rely on warm drinks as preventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious protection claims and refusal to restrict gatherings
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that faith or religious practices (e.g., Holy Communion, prayer) protect against COVID-19 and justify continuing gatherings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious protection claims have led some groups to continue gatherings, resulting in outbreaks (examples in Israel, South Korea, Tanzania, Greece). Such claims conflict with public-health evidence and can increase transmission; medical experts criticized putting religious belief before science when it endangers health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helicopter spraying myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that helicopters spray 'COVID-19 disinfectant' over homes on particular days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No such spraying has taken place or is planned; as of July 2020 there is no agent that could be sprayed to disinfect people/houses in that way. Treat such social-media claims as false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food-related myths (cabbage, Datura, vegetarian immunity)
rubrics_metrics.description: False claims linking particular foods or dietary patterns to immunity or protection from COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: false WHO warning against eating cabbage; Datura fruit ingestion caused hospitalizations after TikTok recommendations; vegetarianism conferring immunity is false. These claims are unsupported and can be dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitamin D claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that vitamin D pills will prevent COVID-19 or that governments suppress vitamin D information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One meta-analysis found weak evidence that higher vitamin D levels may reduce likelihood of ICU admission but no effect on mortality. Evidence is limited and mixed; a fraudulent preprint promoted widely was later discredited. Many social-media videos contained false/misleading vitamin D advice. Do not present vitamin D as a proven preventive or cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vaccine misinformation and hesitancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Various unfounded conspiracy theories and misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines (side effects, immune system misrepresentations, 5G, manufacturing claims, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such misinformation has contributed to vaccine hesitancy. Policymakers introduced incentives and mandates to raise uptake, provoking further misinformation about legality and effects. Critics argue mandates infringe autonomy; scientists promoting vaccination have faced harassment. Accurate, evidence-based vaccine communication is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims about hospital conditions and #FilmYourHospital
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that empty hospital parking lots or videos prove the pandemic is a hoax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite some visible empty lots, many hospitals in places like NYC experienced thousands of COVID-19 hospitalizations. Conspiracy campaigns encouraged filming hospitals to claim a hoax; such selective evidence is misleading and ignores broader data on hospitalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: General warning against unproven treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread social-media claims of treatments that are unproven, scams, or dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many promoted methods are unsupported by evidence and some are dangerous. Distinguish laboratory/cell-culture findings from human clinical evidence; regulatory agencies advise against using unproven therapies outside trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herbal remedies and traditional medicine claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that certain herbs or traditional medicines (e.g., shuanghuanglian, artemisia-based drinks, TCM prescriptions) cure or prevent COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports of in-vitro activity (e.g., Echinacea extracts) do not establish human efficacy. Regulatory agencies have not recommended many herbal remedies for COVID-19. Chinese National Health Commission included TCM in guidelines and it was widely used in China, but such usage does not substitute for rigorous clinical evidence. Exercise caution and require clinical trials and regulatory review before recommending herbal therapies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitamin C for prevention or treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims promoting vitamin C as a cure or treatment for COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vitamin C attracted many warning letters for COVID-19 claims. NIH COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines state there are insufficient data to recommend for or against vitamin C for prevention or treatment in nonhospitalized or hospitalized patients. Do not claim proven benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims equating common cold/flu remedies with COVID cures
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that over-the-counter cold/flu treatments (aspirin, antihistamines, nasal sprays, saline) cure COVID-19 or prove earlier circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbook references to coronaviruses generally do not support claims about SARS-CoV-2 specifically. Saline solutions have no evidence of killing SARS-CoV-2. Early concerns about ibuprofen worsening COVID-19 were not supported; EMA and WHO recommended patients continue ibuprofen as directed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cow dung and urine remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that applying cow dung or drinking cow urine cures COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These claims are false and can lead to harm. Individuals promoting such claims have faced legal action; public-health authorities and scientists criticized politicians/figures who spread them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency approval and misleading claims about 2-Deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 2-DG is WHO-approved or conclusively effective after emergency regulatory approvals in some jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2-DG received emergency-use approval in India as adjunct therapy for moderate to severe patients; claims it was WHO-approved were false. Reports noted the approval was based on poor evidence with no journal publication or preprint available at the time. Scrutinize claims of efficacy and check peer-reviewed data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine cure or prevent COVID-19 in large numbers of patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal/social-media promotion and self-published articles have been misleading; institutions named in such promotions sometimes disavowed affiliation. Regulatory and scientific scrutiny is necessary; unsupported claims have been removed or contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ivermectin claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that ivermectin is effective to treat or prevent COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WHO, EMA, FDA, and IDSA do not advise using ivermectin to treat or prevent COVID-19. Early laboratory research and online advocacy raised interest, and some countries adopted it, but subsequent clinical research failed to confirm benefit; many positive studies were later found faulty, misleading, or fraudulent. Advisories warn against using veterinary formulations. Treat ivermectin promotion skeptically and rely on authoritative guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangerous treatments and 'Miracle' supplements (e.g., MMS/chlorine dioxide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotion of products like Miracle Mineral Supplement (chlorine dioxide) and other hazardous substances as COVID cures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MMS is considered ineffective and dangerous; FDA and law-enforcement actions (raids, legal cases) occurred against promoters. Distribution and ingestion have led to legal consequences and harm. Do not ingest unapproved disinfectants or industrial chemicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant poisonings (Datura/Jimsonweed) from social-media remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents of poisoning after following social-media recommendations to ingest plants like Datura as remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Datura species contain poisonous anticholinergic substances; ingestion led to hospitalizations. Social-media claims recommending such plants are dangerous and false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colloidal silver and other promoted mineral remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims promoting colloidal silver or silver-infused products as COVID treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promoters (e.g., televangelists, radio hosts) were subject to cease-and-desist orders, lawsuits, and regulatory threats. Silver products are not proven cures; authorities have acted against misleading promotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mustard oil / breath-holding test claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that pouring mustard oil through the nose or holding breath for a minute diagnoses or treats COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims (promoted by public figures) are false. Breath-holding is not a diagnostic or protective test; pouring substances up the nose is dangerous and not evidence-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untested/disinfectant injections and UV exposure suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public figures suggesting disinfectant injections or ultraviolet exposure as treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no evidence these are viable or safe treatments. Health authorities warn that such suggestions are dangerous and should not be attempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual healing claims via media
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims by televangelists that they can cure viewers remotely (e.g., by touching screens) or through spiritual practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are unsubstantiated and potentially harmful if they dissuade people from seeking medical care. Treat spiritual-healing cure claims critically and rely on medical evidence for treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organ trafficking and healthcare-worker attack rumors
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseless rumors that people are taken to care centers and killed for organs, leading to protests and attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These false rumors spread rapidly via messaging apps, sparked violence and reduced willingness to seek testing/treatment. Such claims are dangerous misinformation and should be debunked by authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miscellaneous viral falsehoods (name origin, Simpsons 'prediction', wildlife return)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various internet memes and doctored media claiming prophetic predictions or dramatic wildlife/environmental effects attributable to lockdowns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include false derivations of 'COVID-19', doctored Simpsons screenshots, and misattributed wildlife videos/images. Verify provenance of images/video and authoritative naming explanations (WHO's naming explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent virus-infection claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that anyone infected will have the virus in their body permanently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is false: most infected people recover and eliminate the virus. While there is no universal curative treatment, recovery is common; avoid spreading claims of lifelong viral persistence absent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: COVID-19 denialism
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs that the pandemic is faked, exaggerated, or deaths miscounted — i.e., 'COVID is a lie'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denialism is pseudoscience. High-profile individuals have espoused denialist views, which can undermine public health responses. Treat denialist claims critically and rely on established epidemiological data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspiracies fostering antisemitism
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspiracy theories about COVID-19 serving as a gateway to antisemitic rhetoric and 'superconspiracies' tying multiple actors together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports found COVID conspiracies linked to antisemitic narratives (e.g., highlighting Jewish people at leadership positions). Be alert to how public-health conspiracies can feed prejudiced ideologies and call them out.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-run or covert disinformation operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of covert operations to spread anti-vaccine or anti-foreign-vaccine messages (e.g., alleged US operation targeting Chinese vaccine perception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such operations, if conducted, damage public trust and can increase vaccine hesitancy. Scrutinize provenance of social-media accounts and campaigns; recognize that foreign- or state-directed disinformation can affect health outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discouraging use of past tense / ongoing risk messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Language norms about whether to refer to COVID-19 in the past tense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some experts discourage using the past tense because COVID-19 continues to cause acute disease, long COVID, and deaths. WHO Director-General urged against talking about COVID in the past tense, noting ongoing weekly deaths and underreporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efforts to combat the 'infodemic'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of the WHO's 'infodemic' concept and the challenge of abundant false information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WHO described a 'massive infodemic' making it hard for people to find trustworthy sources. Combatting misinformation requires authoritative communication, fact-checking, and supporting reliable guidance.
